metadata.title: Education in Eastern Europe and Central Asia (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The report uses OECD PISA 2018 microdata with a two-stage sampling design selecting at least 150 schools and roughly 42 students per school in each participating country. PISA analyses are typically conducted with complex survey weights to account for unequal selection probabilities and clustering at the school level; however, this report does not specify the exact weight variable names or whether weights were explicitly applied in the authors’ computations. The report also relies on PISA-scaled outcomes (e.g., reading performance and proficiency levels) and on questionnaire-constructed indices (e.g., ESCS, teaching practice indices), which in PISA are produced using the standard PISA scaling framework. For replication or deeper re-analysis, analysts should use the official PISA 2018 student and school weights (and replicate weights if provided) from the PISA database for each country, and apply the standard PISA procedures for combining results across plausible values where applicable.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This is a descriptive policy report synthesizing PISA 2018 results (e.g., mean reading scores, proficiency levels, and associations) rather than an empirical machine-learning study that explicitly documents plausible-value (PV) combination procedures. While PISA outcomes are PV-based in the underlying OECD framework, the report does not provide the PV handling method (e.g., Rubin’s rules) or any missing-data imputation/deletion strategy at the analysis level. Therefore, PV and missing-data handling are not reported in the text provided, and the extraction cannot reliably map them to a specific PV/missing-data procedure.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report focuses on PISA 2018 participants in Eastern Europe and Central Asia supported by UNICEF ECARO and participating in PISA 2018: Azerbaijan (Baku only), Belarus, Bulgaria, Croatia, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Moldova, Romania, Turkey, and Ukraine. PISA 2018 targets 15-year-old students enrolled in Grade 7 or above, using a two-stage sampling procedure selecting at least 150 schools and roughly 42 students per school. The report also notes that some figures/analyses exclude countries due to missing data coverage (e.g., teacher practice indices missing for Ukraine; some figures exclude countries with very small rural shares) and that some analyses restrict populations (e.g., language-of-instruction analysis limited to students speaking the national language at home; meta-cognitive and other indices are based on PISA questionnaire responses). No additional student-level inclusion/exclusion rules (e.g., complete-case rules for missing questionnaire items) are explicitly documented in the provided text.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD/UNICEF report analyzes PISA 2018 to describe education system performance and equity patterns across Eastern Europe and Central Asia (EECA). It uses PISA’s two-stage sampling of schools and students of age 15 (Grade 7 or above) and compares EECA averages to OECD benchmarks, focusing primarily on reading performance and related proficiency levels. The report documents that EECA reading performance is lower than the OECD average (421 vs 487 score points) but generally improving over time, with no decreases among earlier participants. It also highlights inequities: boys score lower than girls in reading (about 32 points on average), urban students outperform rural students with larger gaps than in the OECD, and socio-economic disparities are substantial (about 80 score points between advantaged and disadvantaged students). Beyond achievement, the report synthesizes evidence on school sorting/segregation, resource allocation, learning time, truancy, and teaching practices, translating these patterns into policy considerations for more equitable schooling and teaching.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This record is an OECD/UNICEF policy report that synthesizes PISA 2018 results and related policy evidence rather than presenting an original student-level machine-learning model with documented PV and missing-data procedures. Consequently, there are no ML techniques to extract, no predictive targets, and no model performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/RMSE) to populate. The sparse methodological fields (e.g., PV handling and missing-data handling) reflect that the report communicates descriptive and correlational findings using PISA’s established scaling and reporting framework, without detailing the underlying PV-combination and missing-data workflow in the provided text.
